title: Conjecture 1
statement_text: Every 5-critical graph in ${\cal C}$ contains a vertex of degree four.
context_text: Graphs are simple; ${\cal C}$ is the class of graphs that can be drawn in the plane with at most one crossing (such graphs also embed in the projective plane and the torus), and a graph is $5$-critical if $\chi(G)=5$ and every proper subgraph is $4$-colorable. A subgraph $K$ is separating if $G-V(K)$ is disconnected. Every $5$-critical graph has minimum degree at least four, and degree-four vertices can be handled inductively: if $G\ne K_5$ is $5$-critical with a vertex $v$ of degree four, $v$ has two non-adjacent neighbours $x,y$, and deleting $v$ and identifying $x$ with $y$ gives (when the crossing is not on $vx,vy$) a non-$4$-colorable graph in ${\cal C}$ containing a smaller $5$-critical graph. This conjecture says the base case of this induction is only $K_5$, i.e. there is no $5$-critical graph in ${\cal C}$ of minimum degree at least five; it is supported by computer experiments. The authors' main conjecture states that if $G$ has no separating triangle and has a drawing in the plane with one crossing in which every vertex not incident with the two crossed edges has degree at least five, then $G$ is $4$-colorable; they verify it by computer for all graphs with at most $28$ vertices. Since $5$-critical graphs have no separating cliques, that conjecture implies this one.
paper_title: On a conjecture concerning 4-coloring of graphs with one crossing

title: Conjecture 2
statement_text: If a graph $G$ does not contain separating triangles and has a drawing in the plane with one crossing such that all vertices not incident with the crossed edges have degree at least five, then $G$ is 4-colorable.
context_text: Graphs are simple; a triangle is separating if deleting its vertices disconnects the graph; the condition says that only the (at most four) endpoints of the two crossed edges may have degree less than five. This is the central conjecture of the paper, which the authors verify by computer enumeration for all graphs with at most $28$ vertices. It strengthens the Four Color Theorem to graphs drawable with one crossing under a minimum degree condition, and implies that every $5$-critical graph (i.e. $\chi=5$ and all proper subgraphs $4$-colorable) drawable with at most one crossing has a vertex of degree four, since $5$-critical graphs have no separating cliques. The assumption on separating triangles cannot be dropped: gluing a copy of the icosahedron at each vertex of any graph drawable with one crossing yields such a graph of minimum degree at least five. Consequences include that every graph drawable with one crossing and without the $4$-wheel $W_4$ as a subgraph would be $4$-colorable. Any non-$4$-colorable graph drawn with one crossing has the four endpoints of the crossed edges forming a clique, and the authors reduce the conjecture to showing that no $4$-candidate (a near-triangulation of a disk bounded by a $4$-cycle, with every triangle facial and every internal vertex of degree at least five) forbids all colorings using four distinct colors on its outer $4$-cycle.

title: Conjecture 5
statement_text: Every non-4-colorable graph in ${\cal C}_{0}$ has an internal vertex of degree four.
context_text: Graphs are simple. ${\cal C}_0\subseteq{\cal C}$ consists of the graphs obtained from a $4$-connected plane triangulation by choosing two distinct facial triangles $xuv$ and $yuv$ sharing an edge $uv$ and adding the edge $xy$; $x,y,u,v$ are the external vertices and all others are internal. This is an equivalent form of the authors' main conjecture, that every graph without separating triangles that has a drawing in the plane with one crossing in which all vertices not incident with the crossed edges have degree at least five is $4$-colorable, just as the Four Color Theorem reduces to triangulations. Assuming the main conjecture, the authors show that every non-$4$-colorable graph in ${\cal C}_0$ can be obtained from $K_5$ by a sequence of expansion operations staying among non-$4$-colorable graphs of ${\cal C}_0$, which yields a relatively efficient enumeration algorithm; however, some $5$-critical graphs drawable with one crossing are not in ${\cal C}_0$. The main conjecture is verified by computer for graphs with at most $28$ vertices.

title: Conjecture 30
statement_text: Every bichromatic-forbidding 4-candidate can be obtained from the diamond by a sequence of the operations (A), (B) and (C) described below.
context_text: A canvas is a plane graph whose outer face is bounded by a cycle of length at least four and all of whose other faces are triangles; a $4$-candidate is a canvas whose outer face is bounded by a $4$-cycle $K=x_1x_2x_3x_4$, in which every triangle bounds a face and every internal vertex (not on the outer face) has degree at least five. It is bichromatic-forbidding if it has no $4$-coloring with $\varphi(x_1)=\varphi(x_3)$ and $\varphi(x_2)=\varphi(x_4)$. The diamond is the $4$-cycle with one chord. The three operations, each turning a $4$-candidate $H$ with outer cycle $Q=v_1v_2v_3v_4$ into a larger $4$-candidate $G$ that is bichromatic-forbidding if and only if $H$ is, are: (A) add a cycle $x_1y_1x_2y_2x_3y_3x_4y_4$ around $H$ with edges $v_ix_i$, $v_ix_{i-1}$, $v_iy_{i-1}$, then a new outer $4$-cycle $u_1u_2u_3u_4$ with edges $u_iy_{i-1}$, $u_ix_i$, $u_iy_i$ (indices mod $4$); (B) if $Q$ is induced, add a new outer $4$-cycle $u_1u_2u_3u_4$ with edges $u_iv_i$ and $u_iv_{i+1}$ for all $i$; (C) if $Q$ is induced, $\deg_H v_1,\deg_H v_2\ge5$ and $v_1v_2u_1$ is the inner triangle on the edge $v_1v_2$, delete the edge $v_1v_2$ and add new vertices $u_2,u_3,u_4$ forming the outer $4$-cycle $u_1u_2u_3u_4$ with edges $u_iv_i$, $u_iv_{i+1}$ for $i\in\{2,3,4\}$ ($v_5=v_1$). These candidates arise in the authors' study of their conjecture that graphs without separating triangles, drawn in the plane with one crossing so that all vertices not incident with the crossed edges have degree at least five, are $4$-colorable: by computer enumeration, no $4$-candidate with at most $28$ vertices forbids rainbow colorings (all four colors on $K$), and only the diamond forbids diagonal colorings. In contrast, there are infinitely many bichromatic-forbidding $4$-candidates, produced from the diamond by (A), (B), (C), and the enumeration up to $28$ vertices supports the conjecture that these are all of them.
